quests.hint: Think about a hot drink many people have first thing in the morning.
quests.explanation: 'Coffee' is a popular hot drink made from roasted beans. 'A cup of coffee' is the standard English phrase - not 'a glass' or 'a mug of coffee beans.'
quests.textToSpeak: I always start my day with a hot cup of ___.
quests.correctAnswer: I always start my day with a hot cup of coffee.

quests.hint: This is the most essential drink for staying healthy - it has no colour or taste.
quests.explanation: 'Water' is uncountable in English: 'drink water' not 'drink a water.' We say 'a glass of water' or 'a bottle of water.'
quests.textToSpeak: Doctors recommend drinking at least eight glasses of ___ every day.
quests.correctAnswer: Doctors recommend drinking at least eight glasses of water every day.

quests.hint: This is a baked food made from flour, eaten at almost every meal in many countries.
quests.explanation: 'Bread' is an uncountable noun in English. We say 'a slice of bread' or 'a loaf of bread,' never 'a bread.'
quests.textToSpeak: She buys fresh ___ from the bakery every single morning before work.
quests.correctAnswer: She buys fresh bread from the bakery every single morning before work.

quests.hint: This is the female parent - the woman who gave birth to you or raised you.
quests.explanation: 'Mother' is the formal word; 'mum' (British) or 'mom' (American) are the informal versions used in everyday speech.
quests.textToSpeak: My ___ cooks the most delicious meals I have ever tasted in my life.
quests.correctAnswer: My mother cooks the most delicious meals I have ever tasted in my life.

quests.hint: This is the male sibling - a boy or man who shares the same parents as you.
quests.explanation: 'Brother' is used for male siblings of any age. 'Older brother' and 'younger brother' specify the age relationship. The plural is 'brothers.'
quests.textToSpeak: My ___ and I used to play football together in the park every weekend.
quests.correctAnswer: My brother and I used to play football together in the park every weekend.

quests.hint: This word refers to all your close relatives - parents, siblings, grandparents.
quests.explanation: 'Family' can be used with singular or plural verbs depending on context: 'my family is' (unit) or 'my family are' (members). Both are correct in British English.
quests.textToSpeak: We always gather as a ___ for Sunday dinner at my grandmother's house.
quests.correctAnswer: We always gather as a family for Sunday dinner at my grandmother's house.

quests.hint: Think of a physical activity that involves moving on foot at a relaxed pace.
quests.explanation: 'Walk' is a regular verb: walk, walked, walked. 'Go for a walk' (noun) and 'walk to work' (verb) are the most common patterns.
quests.textToSpeak: I like to ___ to work when the weather is warm and the sun is shining.
quests.correctAnswer: I like to walk to work when the weather is warm and the sun is shining.

quests.hint: This is what you do with a book, magazine, or article to understand its content.
quests.explanation: 'Read' is an irregular verb: read (present), read /red/ (past). 'Read a book' and 'read to someone' are the main patterns in English.
quests.textToSpeak: She loves to ___ novels in bed before going to sleep at night.
quests.correctAnswer: She loves to read novels in bed before going to sleep at night.

quests.hint: This is the skill of preparing and making food using heat.
quests.explanation: 'Cook' can be a verb ('I cook dinner') or a noun ('She is a great cook'). 'Cook a meal' and 'cook for someone' are the most natural patterns.
quests.textToSpeak: He learned to ___ many traditional dishes during his year living in Italy.
quests.correctAnswer: He learned to cook many traditional dishes during his year living in Italy.

quests.hint: This is the room in a house where food is prepared and meals are cooked.
quests.explanation: 'Kitchen' is the standard word for the cooking area in a home. In British English, we say 'in the kitchen,' not 'at the kitchen.'
quests.textToSpeak: We spend most of our evenings in the ___, preparing meals and chatting.
quests.correctAnswer: We spend most of our evenings in the kitchen, preparing meals and chatting.

quests.hint: This is the room in a house where you sleep and keep your personal belongings.
quests.explanation: 'Bedroom' is one word in English. We say 'in my bedroom,' not 'at my bedroom.' A 'double bedroom' has space for two people.
quests.textToSpeak: My ___ has a large window with a beautiful view of the park outside.
quests.correctAnswer: My bedroom has a large window with a beautiful view of the park outside.

quests.hint: This is an outdoor area attached to a house where plants and flowers are grown.
quests.explanation: 'Garden' is the British English word; Americans say 'yard.' 'In the garden' is the correct preposition - never 'on the garden.'
quests.textToSpeak: She planted roses and sunflowers in the ___ at the start of spring.
quests.correctAnswer: She planted roses and sunflowers in the garden at the start of spring.

quests.hint: This describes a feeling of joy and satisfaction - the opposite of sad.
quests.explanation: 'Happy' is an adjective: 'I am happy,' 'She looks happy.' The adverb is 'happily.' 'Feel happy about' something is a very common English structure.
quests.textToSpeak: She felt very ___ when she heard that she had passed all her exams.
quests.correctAnswer: She felt very happy when she heard that she had passed all her exams.

quests.hint: This describes a state of exhaustion - when you have no energy left at all.
quests.explanation: 'Tired' is an adjective: 'I feel tired.' We say 'tired of' (bored by something) or 'tired from' (exhausted due to something).
quests.textToSpeak: After the long journey, we were all completely ___ and needed to rest.
quests.correctAnswer: After the long journey, we were all completely tired and needed to rest.

quests.hint: This describes a feeling of eager anticipation - when something wonderful is about to happen.
quests.explanation: 'Excited' is an adjective: 'I am excited about the trip.' Don't confuse it with 'exciting' (which describes the thing, not the person's feeling).
quests.textToSpeak: The children were absolutely ___ about the trip to the theme park.
quests.correctAnswer: The children were absolutely excited about the trip to the theme park.

quests.hint: This adjective describes weather when there is bright light from the sun in the sky.
quests.explanation: 'Sunny' is an adjective derived from 'sun.' 'A sunny day' means clear skies and bright sunshine. 'It's sunny outside' is more common than 'the sun is out.'
quests.textToSpeak: It was a beautiful ___ day, perfect for a picnic in the countryside.
quests.correctAnswer: It was a beautiful sunny day, perfect for a picnic in the countryside.

quests.hint: This adjective describes a low temperature - the opposite of hot or warm.
quests.explanation: 'Cold' describes temperatures below normal comfort levels. 'Cold weather,' 'a cold day,' 'feel cold' are the key collocations. 'It's cold outside' is very common.
quests.textToSpeak: Make sure you wear a warm coat because it is very ___ outside today.
quests.correctAnswer: Make sure you wear a warm coat because it is very cold outside today.

quests.hint: This is an object you carry over your head to stay dry when it is raining.
quests.explanation: 'Umbrella' is always countable: 'an umbrella,' 'my umbrella.' 'Take your umbrella' and 'carry an umbrella' are the most natural collocations in English.
quests.textToSpeak: Do not forget to take your ___ - the forecast says it will rain all day.
quests.correctAnswer: Do not forget to take your umbrella - the forecast says it will rain all day.

quests.hint: This is the device most people carry with them everywhere to call and send messages.
quests.explanation: 'Phone' can mean a mobile phone or landline. 'On your phone' (using it) and 'by phone' (via phone call) are both common structures in English.
quests.textToSpeak: She sent a quick message on her ___ to say she was running a bit late.
quests.correctAnswer: She sent a quick message on her phone to say she was running a bit late.

quests.hint: This is a container with handles that you carry your belongings in when you go out.
quests.explanation: 'Bag' is a general word. 'Handbag' (woman's bag), 'backpack' (rucksack), and 'shopping bag' are more specific. 'In your bag' is the correct preposition.
quests.textToSpeak: He packed all his books and supplies into his ___ before leaving for school.
quests.correctAnswer: He packed all his books and supplies into his bag before leaving for school.

quests.hint: This is a small metal object used to open or lock a door.
quests.explanation: 'Key' is countable: 'a key,' 'my keys.' 'Key to the door' and 'spare key' are common collocations. 'Lose your keys' is one of the most frequent English complaints!
quests.textToSpeak: I could not find my ___ and had to wait outside the flat for an hour.
quests.correctAnswer: I could not find my key and had to wait outside the flat for an hour.

quests.hint: This is the first meal of the day, usually eaten in the morning.
quests.explanation: 'Breakfast' is uncountable when referring to the general meal: 'I had breakfast' (no article). But 'a big breakfast' uses an article when you describe it.
quests.textToSpeak: Nutritionists agree that ___ is the most important meal of the day.
quests.correctAnswer: Nutritionists agree that breakfast is the most important meal of the day.

quests.hint: This is the midday meal, eaten around the middle of the day.
quests.explanation: 'Lunch' is usually uncountable: 'have lunch,' 'go for lunch,' 'at lunchtime.' 'Grab some lunch' is an informal phrase. 'Lunch break' is a common compound noun.
quests.textToSpeak: We usually have ___ together in the canteen at about one o'clock.
quests.correctAnswer: We usually have lunch together in the canteen at about one o'clock.

quests.hint: This is the main evening meal, usually the largest meal of the day.
quests.explanation: 'Dinner' or 'supper' refers to the evening meal. 'Have dinner,' 'cook dinner,' and 'go out for dinner' are the most common collocations in British English.
quests.textToSpeak: The whole family sat down together for ___ at seven o'clock on Sundays.
quests.correctAnswer: The whole family sat down together for dinner at seven o'clock on Sundays.

quests.hint: This is the medical professional you visit when you are unwell or need a check-up.
quests.explanation: 'See a doctor' and 'go to the doctor's' are the most natural English phrases. 'Doctor's surgery' (British) or 'doctor's office' (American) refers to their workplace.
quests.textToSpeak: If you are feeling unwell, you should see a ___ as soon as possible.
quests.correctAnswer: If you are feeling unwell, you should see a doctor as soon as possible.

quests.hint: This is the place where children go to learn, taught by qualified teachers.
quests.explanation: 'At school' (studying there) is different from 'at the school' (at the building). 'Go to school,' 'start school,' and 'leave school' are key collocations.
quests.textToSpeak: The children walk to ___ together every morning, rain or shine.
quests.correctAnswer: The children walk to school together every morning, rain or shine.

quests.hint: This is a public building where books, magazines, and resources can be borrowed for free.
quests.explanation: 'At the library' or 'in the library' are both correct. 'Borrow' (take temporarily) is used for library books, not 'rent.' Libraries are a free public resource.
quests.textToSpeak: She spent the afternoon in the ___ quietly studying for her history exam.
quests.correctAnswer: She spent the afternoon in the library quietly studying for her history exam.

quests.hint: This adjective describes something that is very pleasing to look at.
quests.explanation: 'Beautiful' intensifies with 'absolutely' - 'absolutely beautiful.' It describes people, places, and things. 'Gorgeous' is a slightly more informal synonym.
quests.textToSpeak: The view from the top of the mountain was absolutely ___ on a clear day.
quests.correctAnswer: The view from the top of the mountain was absolutely beautiful on a clear day.

quests.hint: This adjective describes food or drink that has a wonderful, enjoyable taste.
quests.explanation: 'Delicious' is used specifically for food and drink. 'Absolutely delicious' and 'smell delicious' are common. It is stronger than 'tasty' or 'nice.'
quests.textToSpeak: The pasta they served at the local restaurant was absolutely ___.
quests.correctAnswer: The pasta they served at the local restaurant was absolutely delicious.

quests.hint: This adjective describes something that costs a lot of money - more than you can afford.
quests.explanation: 'Expensive' collocates with 'too,' 'very,' and 'rather.' 'Far too expensive' is a very common emphasis. The opposite is 'cheap' or 'affordable.'
quests.textToSpeak: The jacket was lovely but far too ___ for what I could afford right now.
quests.correctAnswer: The jacket was lovely but far too expensive for what I could afford right now.
